beats.narration_text: Namaste. I'm Siddhesh Nikam, and this is the pitch for my final project. Lots of tools will answer a data question. My question is different. Can I prove the answer is right?

my campaign questions?

beats.narration_text: Three terms. ROAS, return on ad spend: revenue divided by what the ads cost. A prompt contract: the fixed rules I give Claude about what it may write, and in what form. And a test set: questions whose right answers I work out by hand, before Claude sees them.

fixed rules that limit what Claude will write
questions I solve by hand first: the key

beats.narration_text: Here is the project in one sentence. CheckedSQL will let a marketing analyst ask a question in plain English, have Claude write the S Q L, run it on a campaign database, and show the answer with the query and a check.

beats.narration_text: When it's done, it will be a GitHub repository with four things. A synthetic campaign dataset. The question tool, written in Python. A test set of about thirty questions. And an evaluation log that records every pass and every miss.

beats.narration_text: I looked at two real alternatives. The first is one I built: a Tableau dashboard for my marketing campaign project. It answers the questions I planned in advance. A new question means building a new view.

beats.narration_text: The second is pasting a question into a general chat assistant. It writes a query, and some can run code on an uploaded file, but there's no fixed test set, so no record of how often it's right on my questions. CheckedSQL's difference: every answer is run, shown with its query, and scored against answers I checked by hand.

beats.narration_text: The target role is data analyst, and the first reader is a hiring manager. In the first sixty seconds, they'll open the README, see the score table from the test set, and run one command that prints the query, the answer, and whether it matched.

beats.narration_text: What will it prove? That I write S Q L and define marketing metrics correctly, which I already do. And that I can use what this course teaches: a prompt contract, verification against known answers, and a repeatable evaluation. The evidence: the test set, the log, and a write-up of every failure.

beats.narration_text: What's out. It will not change the database. It will only run read-only queries, on this one campaign schema. No dashboards, and no real company data.

beats.narration_text: What comes first: the test set and the checker, before any Claude call. I'll write ten questions, work out their answers by hand, and run my own queries through the checker as a baseline. You'll know it ran when one command prints a score table. Then Claude gets the same ten.

beats.narration_text: What could sink it: an answer that looks right but isn't. ROAS is a ratio. Average it row by row, and you get a different number than total revenue over total spend, and both look plausible. My fix: put the metric definitions in the prompt contract, and add ratio questions to the test set, so this mistake gets caught and logged.

shot.visual_intent: Two grey bars of different heights labelled 'row average' and 'total ÷ total'; a check lands on the total bar and a test page slides in.

beats.narration_text: Why this project? It's a mix. S Q L, PostgreSQL and pandas, I already have. My marketing campaign analytics repository on GitHub computes click-through rate and return on ad spend with them. New to me are calling Claude from Python, writing prompt contracts, and building an evaluation harness. That's the part I'm here to learn.

beats.narration_text: What exists today: my two earlier GitHub repositories, and this pitch. Nothing of CheckedSQL is built yet. The dataset, the tool, the test set and the log will exist. What I don't know yet is whether thirty questions is enough. I'll find out by watching whether new questions keep finding new kinds of failure.
